evidence: Phaedr. 5.9.2: cum vix intrāre posset ad praesēpia
Cic. Phil. 2.68: tū illud sānctissimum līmen intrāre? (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Phil. 2.68: tū ingredī illam domum ausus es? (Lewis & Short)

terms.comment: intrō īre, to go in; also written as one word, as in Terence’s intrōībās.

Intus is “inside”, of rest; with a verb of motion classical Latin says intrō: abī intrō (Plaut. Aul. 89). Lewis & Short notes intus for intrō as rare and doubtful, “cf. Quint. 1.5.50”, where it is cited as a fault. Say Ī intrō!.

phrases.latin: Quis hīc loquitur? ehem, tūne hīc erās, mī Phaedria? Quid hīc stābās? cūr nōn rēctā intrōībās?
phrases.english: who’s that talking? Oh, is it you, Phaedria dear? Why were you standing out here? Why didn’t you come straight in?
why are you standing there? Go on in!

phrases.latin: angustō in aditū taurus luctāns cornibus cum vix intrāre posset ad praesēpia
phrases.english: a bull, struggling with his horns in a narrow doorway, could hardly get in to his stall

phrases.latin: abī intrō, occlūde jānuam. jam ego hīc erō.
phrases.english: go in, shut the door, I’ll be right back.
